title: {{NAME}} and the Valley Where Time Stood Still
moral: Some places are precious because they are unspoiled, and protecting them is a gift to the future.

pages.content:
The valley had no name on any map.

{{NAME}}'s grandmother had called it the Still Valley, and written only this: go once, look carefully, tell no one.

He went on a Saturday in early spring.

In the valley: a small herd of Diplodocus, grazing in morning mist. A family of red foxes watching from a rock. Rabbits everywhere. And at the valley's centre, still and white, a unicorn whose horn cast the light of stars.

pages.content:
The unicorn's name was Lore and she was, she explained (in the way unicorns do, with images and feeling), the valley's keeper.

She had maintained the equilibrium for centuries: the Diplodocus needed the large ferns, the foxes needed the rabbits, the rabbits needed the grass, and all of them needed quiet and safety.

Her concern: the valley was changing. A slow change, almost invisible, but she felt it.

"The spring came three days earlier this year," she said.

{{NAME}} took out his notebook.

pages.content:
He spent three visits documenting: plant flowering times, animal behaviour, the temperature of the spring. Lore guided him to the places that had changed most.

The Diplodocus, meanwhile, had accepted him after the second visit, treating him with the particular casualness that very large creatures reserve for things that are obviously not a threat.

One young one followed him constantly, sniffing his notebook.

"He thinks it's food," said Lore.

"It's research," said {{NAME}}.

"He doesn't know the difference yet," said Lore.

No text, no words, no letters anywhere in the image.

pages.content:
His data showed: the valley's underground spring had shifted slightly, changing the water available to the ferns.

Fewer ferns meant less food for the Diplodocus. Less Diplodocus movement meant less ground disturbance. Less disturbance meant fewer rabbit burrows, which meant less habitat diversity.

The chain of connections was delicate and specific.

"We need to redirect the spring slightly," {{NAME}} said. "Back to its original path."

Lore's horn glowed. She showed him where: a point where old rock had shifted.

They worked together: her magic, his hands.

pages.content:
By late afternoon, the spring flowed as it had.

{{NAME}} sat on the valley edge and watched the Diplodocus move toward the ferns at the rerouted spring. The foxes settled. The rabbits emerged.

Lore stood beside him and her horn was quiet now, just silver in the evening air.

"You'll come back," she said. Not a question.

"Every spring," said {{NAME}}. "To check."

He walked home as the stars came out, carrying his notebook full of the valley's secrets, and keeping them exactly as his grandmother had asked.
